title: Cold rebuild: PEM by hand
summary: Rebuild PEM by hand from memory, no hints.

steps.title: Cold rebuild
body: Time to prove a piece stuck. You built **PEM by hand** in *PEM, DER and PFX*. Now write it again from an
**empty editor**: no starter, no hints, no solution to peek at. The tests are exactly the ones you passed
Why: pulling something out of memory is what makes it stay there. Reading your old code feels like knowing
it; rebuilding it cold shows whether you do. If you get stuck, that is useful news: go back to the lesson,
then come back and try again tomorrow.
This check, plus the boss, is what proves the module.

steps.prompt: `ExportCertificatePem()` wraps the DER bytes in PEM. What does this print?
code: using var cert = new CertificateRequest("CN=demo", key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256).CreateSelfSigned(
steps.explain: DER always begins with `0x30` (an ASN.1 SEQUENCE). Base64 of `30 82 ...` starts with `MII`, which is why almost every PEM certificate body begins with those letters.

steps.title: Rebuild PEM by hand cold
prompt: PEM is simple enough to write yourself. Write `string ToPem(byte[] der)` that returns:
<Base64 of der, broken into lines of 64 characters>
Join lines with `\n` and add no trailing newline. The last Base64 line may be shorter than 64.
**Run checks** compares your output with .NET's own `ExportCertificatePem()`.
**From memory this time:** the editor starts empty and the tests are the ones you passed in the lesson.
